events.arc: Single email: open on the gap between knowing how many signups you got and knowing what produced them, name the concrete first step (a signup goal, pageview type, no code), show what the dashboard then breaks down, and hand them the official guide to set it up or review what they have.

emails.job: Get the reader to set up or review a trial-signup conversion goal by reading the official goal-conversions guide.
emails.single_idea: Set up a signup conversion goal and Plausible stops showing you just a signup total and starts showing which sources and landing pages produced those signups.
emails.objection: Setting up conversion tracking sounds like it means editing my site's code.
must_not_say: Do not presume the reader currently uses Google Analytics or any named analytics tool, and do not pitch a switch or import
Do not presume their traffic volume or reference pageview limits or pricing tiers
Do not presume their privacy-compliance status or lead on cookieless/GDPR as their reason to act
Do not claim or imply a measured lift (the 84% rise or the 2.65%-to-4.80% figures) — those came from Plausible editing its own homepage, not from installing Plausible
Do not promise to fix trial-to-paid conversion or payment-method failures (P3) — that is out of scope and unsupported
Do not state what a 'good' conversion rate is or offer a benchmark for the reader's own traffic

Plausible can only record a paid conversion if the owner sends it as a backend event, revenue attribution sits on the Business plan, and the ledger contains nothing about in-trial product usage or billing, so the measurement stops at.

The 2.65% to 4.80% lift (E11) came from Plausible editing its own homepage, not from installing Plausible; the product locates entry pages and drop-off steps and the owner still has to make the change and re-measure.
emails.felt_need: Free-trial signups do not convert to paid at a rate the owner considers acceptable, even after a signup surge.
emails.status_quo: They add free trials that require a payment method upfront to try to convert website visitors into paying customers.
emails.why_it_fails: A running total doesn't attribute anything — it can't tell you which referrer or which entry page produced the signups, so you're editing pages without knowing which ones convert.
emails.mechanism: You define a goal for the trial signup — the simplest is a pageview goal on the page a visitor lands on right after registering, which needs no code because pageviews are already collected. Once it's set and the first conversion records, it appears in the Goals section, and clicking it breaks the signups down by referrer source and entry page.
emails.call_to_action: Read the official goal-conversions guide to set up or review your signup goal (https://plausible.io/docs/goal-conversions).
emails.next_step_decision: Whether and how to configure a trial-signup goal — which goal type to use and what it will report.
emails.next_step_value: The guide shows the two goal types, that a pageview goal needs no code, and that once a goal is set the dashboard reports conversions by referrer source and entry page.
emails.next_step_limit: The guide explains how to set up and read a goal; it does not tell the reader what counts as a good conversion rate, nor does it address trial-to-paid or payment-failure issues.

events.body:
You can see which **sources and landing pages** drive your trial signups — not just how many there are.

That's what Plausible Analytics does. It's a privacy-friendly web analytics dashboard, and once you set up a conversion goal for your trial signup, a raw count turns into the referrer sources and entry pages that produced it.

You might expect that to mean editing your site's code. The simplest goal doesn't. A pageview goal watches the page a visitor lands on right after registering, and pageviews are already collected — so **no code changes**.

Once it's set and the first conversion records, the goal shows up in the Goals section of your dashboard. Click it, and the signups break down by source and entry page.

The official goal-conversions guide walks through both goal types and what each one reports — a good place to set up a new goal or review one you already have.

events.body:
After a launch or a change to your signup flow, you watch the trial signups climb. That total answers how many. It can't say which referrer or which landing page sent them.

So you end up editing pages without knowing which ones actually convert.

Plausible is a privacy-friendly web analytics dashboard. Set up a signup conversion goal and it stops showing you one number and starts showing **which sources and landing pages** produced those signups.

If that sounds like it means touching your site's code, it doesn't. The simplest version is a pageview goal on the page a visitor lands on right after registering — and because pageviews are collected automatically, it needs **no code**.

Once the goal is set and the first conversion records, it shows up in the Goals section. Click it, and the signups break down by referrer source and entry page.

The official guide walks through both goal types, shows why a pageview goal needs no code, and explains what the dashboard reports once a goal is live.

That's the decision it helps you make: which goal type to use, and what it will tell you.

events.body:
You can rewrite a landing page and still not know whether it's the one bringing in your trial signups.

Plausible Analytics is a privacy-friendly web analytics dashboard. Set up a goal for your trial signup and a raw count turns into **the referrer sources and entry pages** that produced it — the conversion rate, and the top pages people convert on.

Two goal types do this. A custom event goal takes a small snippet. A pageview goal takes none: once Plausible's script is on your site, pageviews are collected automatically — so the page people reach right after registering becomes a goal with **no code**.

Which type fits your signup flow, and what each one reports, is what the official goal-conversions guide walks through. Read it to set up a new signup goal, or to review the one you already have.

readers.persona:
Selected audience (explicit constraints): Small SaaS website owner measuring signup conversion.
The context and problem reports below describe observed members of this market, not established experiences or installed tools of this recipient. The campaign request controls which job this email addresses; do not require a link to an unrequested integration in your doubts or click requirements.
Observed context (grounded; applicability must be checked): Small SaaS website owners who already have a live product with public pricing and signup pages, and who track and publicly report their own visitor-to-signup and trial-to-paid conversion numbers, often after a launch spike or after changing their signup flow.
Source: https://www.indiehackers.com/post/what-is-a-free-trial-paid-conversion-rate-for-a-saas-5ca40ae619; quote: Hey everyone, lately we've finished first place on Product Hunt and got 300 hundred signups.
Source: https://www.indiehackers.com/post/miserable-free-trial-conversion-rate-c0ddeab048; quote: It's a huge success in terms of new sign-ups (roughly +500%), but miserable in terms of conversion to paid customers, even though they need to provide a payment method upfront.
Problem context: Free-trial signups do not convert to paid at a rate the owner considers acceptable, even after a signup surge.; source: https://www.indiehackers.com/post/what-is-a-free-trial-paid-conversion-rate-for-a-saas-5ca40ae619
Problem context: Website visitor-to-signup conversion can stay flat and low despite months of continued feature development.; source: https://www.indiehackers.com/post/after-4-landing-page-rewrites-i-finally-figured-out-why-my-analytics-saas-wasnt-converting-1d5b9be9b0
Problem context: Trial users who do not cancel still fail to become paying customers because their payment method fails at charge time.; source: https://www.indiehackers.com/post/miserable-free-trial-conversion-rate-c0ddeab048
Problem context: Owners lack a clear, agreed-upon benchmark for what counts as a good visitor-to-signup or trial-to-paid conversion rate for their own traffic.; source: https://www.indiehackers.com/post/what-is-a-free-trial-paid-conversion-rate-for-a-saas-5ca40ae619
readers.what_it_sells: A privacy-friendly web analytics dashboard (Plausible) that lets me set a signup 'goal' so I can see which referrer sources and entry pages produce my trial signups, plus the conversion rate per page.
readers.biggest_doubt: Adopting this means putting their analytics script on my site — effort and possibly replacing or doubling up on whatever I use now, and the email doesn't say whether it fits alongside my current setup or what it costs.
readers.stopped_at: Two goal types do this. A custom event goal takes a small snippet.
fixes: 'Read it to set up a new signup goal, or to review the one you already have.' — assumes I'm already a Plausible user; split the ask for someone who isn't on it yet.

'A custom event goal takes a small snippet. A pageview goal takes none...' — this got dense on a busy morning; lead with the no-code pageview goal as the one-minute first step and drop the custom-event detail into the guide.
Add one line on price/trial and whether it coexists with an existing analytics tool, since that's the real blocker to clicking.
